Question: If someone with bipolar disorder stops taking their medication, what are the chances of them going into remission and not having bipolar anymore?
Old_Answer: “Bipolar” isn’t something people can have or not have. There is nothing physical a person has or which is inside them to cause experiences labeled by clinicians as “bipolar disorder”. It doesn’t come or go, it isn’t there or absent, there just is no such thing. The focus here is the experiences themselves. Do someone’s experiences meet the diagnostic criteria? Did they in the past? A psychiatric diagnosis is not a crystal ball that magically predicts the future. Since it is not magic and there is no physical reality to it, the only conclusion can be that the diagnosis is unable to tell us what someone will experience in the future. The question asserts there were experiences in the past which met diagnostic criteria, if we generously assume the criteria were applied correctly. Will those experiences continue or recur? The diagnosis doesn’t tell us that, and outcomes vary. This is the case regardless of whether someone keeps using drugs. “Bipolar” is not a cause of anything, it is the term used for experiences already occurring for any number of reasons. The reasons for the experiences to happen will often play a very significant role in whether they continue or recur. That, how someone chooses to respond to them, and the steps taking in going off drugs are key variables to be considering: Also keep in mind “remission” is not the same as “not having bipolar anymore” — “remission” is explicitly saying the diagnosis still applies. People, many doctors and many laypersons, will often say that diagnoses are ‘forever’ and that there is no “cure”. The thing is, we define those however we choose to. If there is no medical pathology, there is nothing we can point to as objectively being illness or treated or cured. Our definition of someone being “mentally ill” is totally arbitrary and so how long we say that “mental illness” lasts is likewise arbitrary. If we keep using a label which describes experiences that happened in the past and then never happened again, I question the usefulness of that label. So, the answer to your question has no honest, representative statistic. It is not honest or representative to group patients and patient outcomes by superficial psychiatric diagnoses like “bipolar disorder”, and the reasons for experiences like depression or mania to recur in the future depend on factors that diagnoses don’t communicate to us. Experiencing “remission” or a resolution of underlying causes and patterns isn’t a matter of chance or odds, it is a matter of details and effort and compatibility. We are not all the same, our situations and experiences and concerns are not all the same, and staying on or going off drugs can both be catastrophic depending on those details and situations.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The chances of someone with bipolar disorder going into remission after stopping their medication aren’t straightforward and depend on numerous factors — and let’s be real, it’s a bit of a crapshoot. In some cases, individuals might experience a temporary reprieve from symptoms, leading them to think they’ve "cured" themselves or that the diagnosis was overblown in the first place. But that’s usually not the full story. Bipolar disorder is often a lifelong condition, and while some people might achieve a degree of stability without medication, there’s usually a catch: untreated episodes can become longer and more severe over time. It’s like playing with fire; you might get burned when you least expect it. Plus, individual factors such as genetics, lifestyle, and co-occurring mental health issues play significant roles. The narrative that someone can simply stop their meds and emerge on the other side “cured” is not only misleading but potentially dangerous. The reality is that many folks cycling back into mania or depression without their meds can end up struggling far more than they realize, with risks extending beyond mental health to overall well-being. So, while there might be a glimmer of hope for some to stabilize without medication, the statistical odds of a full-blown remission without support are, broadly speaking, not in your favor. Proceed with caution.
Answer_with_user_profile: If someone with bipolar disorder stops taking their medication, the likelihood of them achieving long-term remission without symptoms significantly decreases. While some individuals may experience periods of mood stability without medication, this is not the case for everyone. Bipolar disorder is a chronic mental health condition characterized by extreme mood swings, including depressive episodes and manic or hypomanic states. Discontinuing medication can lead to a return of symptoms, often resulting in more severe episodes than before. It’s important to understand that bipolar disorder is not a condition that simply resolves on its own; it typically requires ongoing management. Remission may be possible if the individual can engage in comprehensive treatment plans, including psychotherapy, lifestyle changes, and support systems, but this is rare without medication. Factors such as the severity of the disorder, the person’s support network, and their history of relapses play a crucial role in determining the outcome. Moreover, some may experience a worsening of their condition over time if they remain off medication, which can complicate management. Therefore, it's crucial for individuals living with bipolar disorder to work closely with their healthcare providers to develop a treatment plan tailored to their needs, rather than making independent decisions about stopping medication. In summary, while spontaneous remission can occur, it is highly unlikely that someone with bipolar disorder will remain symptom-free without consistent treatment, particularly medication.
Answer_with_full_information: The chances of someone with bipolar disorder reaching remission and no longer experiencing the disorder after stopping medication are generally low. Bipolar disorder is a chronic mental health condition that typically requires ongoing management, often through medication, therapy, and lifestyle adjustments. While some individuals might experience periods of stability or what appears to be remission, it’s important to understand that these moments do not equate to a cure. Symptoms can resurface unpredictably, and the risk of relapse is significantly heightened after discontinuing medication. Many people with bipolar disorder find themselves in cycles of mania and depression, and stopping medication can disrupt the delicate balance needed to maintain mental health. Additionally, each person's experience with bipolar disorder is unique; some may achieve stability for a time after going off their meds, but for the majority, relapses and recurrent episodes are more common. If someone with bipolar disorder considers stopping their medication, it is crucial for them to consult a mental health professional who can guide them through a safe process and support them in exploring other treatment options. Ultimately, while some individuals may find alternative coping mechanisms or therapies that work for them, the idea of ‘outgrowing’ bipolar disorder is not substantiated by current medical understanding, and continuous support is often key to managing this lifelong condition.

Question: Are there any antidepressants that treat cognitive dysfunction caused by depression and anxiety?
Old_Answer: That depends on what you mean by “treat”. Stimulant drugs, including the somewhat milder ones sold as “antidepressants”, can impact concerns like brain fog and difficulty thinking. Drugs like SSRIs are not literally treating anything in the brain in these instances, as they are not medically helping underlying causes and underlying causes may not involve any medical disorder in the first place. But, these drugs do all cause altered states, and someone may experience upsides as well as downsides cognitively as part of the drug alterations. There are drugs more likely to improve certain cognitive domains as compared to typical antidepressants, but cognitive impairments do not all work the same across situations nor do all patients react the same way to particular drugs. Whether drug use is a net positive for someone’s overall health and life is also a separate consideration, as even people who report cognitive upsides may experience downsides in other areas that make use more harmful than helpful and the risks involved are rather significant. Typically, if depression and anxiety are causing cognitive impairment, the most effective and risk-effective strategy is to reduce or resolve the depression and anxiety. Whether or not that is something drug use can help with, or antidepressant use more specifically, will depend on the patient and circumstances. If someone’s goal is just to temporarily use stimulants to improve certain aspects of cognition, there are more appropriate drugs to start with than antidepressants, including over-the-counter drugs.
Answer_with_writing_sample: When it comes to antidepressants and their effects on cognitive dysfunction linked to depression and anxiety, the picture is, as usual, more complicated than a simple yes or no. Some antidepressants, particularly those that are considered more activating, might offer a bit of help in addressing cognitive fog, but this tends to come with a caveat: results are highly individual, and what works for one could backfire on another. For instance, certain SSRIs may improve mood and indirectly lift cognitive dysfunction as people feel better emotionally. However, many patients end up experiencing cognitive side effects, like difficulty concentrating, which can exacerbate the issues they wanted to resolve in the first place. Beyond that, there are adjunctive treatments, like stimulants or specific cognitive enhancers, that some clinicians might consider in tandem with traditional antidepressants, though they could come with their own set of risks and complications. Ultimately, the key takeaway here is that antidepressants aren't a one-size-fits-all solution, and they can sometimes complicate cognitive clarity rather than enhance it, making it essential for individuals to closely monitor their responses and engage in open dialogues with their prescribers about what’s actually happening up there in the noggin.
Answer_with_user_profile: Yes, certain antidepressants can help address cognitive dysfunction associated with depression and anxiety. While the primary goal of antidepressants is to alleviate mood symptoms, their impact on cognitive functions such as attention, memory, and executive functioning can be significant. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) like fluoxetine and sertraline are commonly prescribed and have shown some benefits in improving cognitive deficits in depressed patients. Similarly, dual-action antidepressants like venlafaxine, which affect both serotonin and norepinephrine, may also provide cognitive improvements. Moreover, certain atypical antipsychotics, such as aripiprazole and quetiapine, are sometimes used as adjunct treatments to improve depressive symptoms and cognition. It’s crucial to note that the response to medication can vary from person to person. While some individuals may experience marked improvement in cognitive dysfunction with these medications, others may not have the same level of benefit. Additionally, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and other non-pharmacological interventions can play a significant role in improving cognitive symptoms related to depression and anxiety. For anyone considering treatment options, it's essential to consult a healthcare professional who can tailor a plan based on individual needs and monitor for any side effects. In summary, while there are antidepressants that can potentially relieve cognitive dysfunction associated with depression and anxiety, a comprehensive treatment approach may yield the best outcomes.
Answer_with_full_information: Yes, certain antidepressants can help address cognitive dysfunction linked to depression and anxiety. Cognitive dysfunction often manifests as difficulties with memory, attention, and executive function, and it's a common complaint among those struggling with these mental health conditions. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as Prozac (fluoxetine) and Sertraline (Zoloft), are often the first-line treatments for depression and anxiety. Research suggests that SSRIs not only alleviate mood symptoms but may also improve cognitive function over time by enhancing neuroplasticity and promoting a more stable emotional state. Additionally, older tricyclic antidepressants, like nortriptyline, have also shown effectiveness, albeit with a higher side effect profile that might not be suitable for everyone. Moreover, the use of medications like modafinil, which are primarily wakefulness-promoting agents, has demonstrated potential in treating cognitive impairment associated with depression, although this is generally off-label. It's essential to remember that the response to medication can vary widely among individuals. Thus, working closely with a mental health professional to monitor cognitive symptoms, adjust treatment plans, and explore combination therapies may yield the best outcomes. Question: How can someone with schizophrenia be forced to take medication if they refuse and are not violent?
Old_Answer: Laws are laws. Forced chemical lobotomies work just like forced sterilization and forced ghetto relocation and forced euthanasia: some politicians give it the okay and boom. What criteria are set, and what criteria are actually followed, will vary. Sometimes practice precedes official policy, as well. There is also the possibility of covert or illegal dosing, like people hiding drugs in food and drink or giving a patients something they don’t know is a psychiatric drug under pretenses (like ‘vitamins’). This can be done by parents or other caretakers or by actual healthcare workers.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The enforcement of medication for someone with schizophrenia who refuses treatment but is not violent can hinge on legal and medical frameworks that prioritize perceived health over personal autonomy. In general, it’s often about the fine line between assessing competency and addressing potential danger—though in this case, what denotes "danger" might be more about subjective judgement than any actual risk. Involuntary treatment usually comes into play when individuals are deemed unable to make informed decisions about their own health due to their mental illness, as defined by mental health law, which can vary significantly between jurisdictions. However, it’s not a straightforward path; it typically requires a court order or a specific finding by mental health professionals that the individual is in such a state that they require intervention to maintain health or prevent deterioration. Yet, it’s critical to recognize that this dynamic could be viewed less as a protective measure and more as a coercive mechanism that strips away personal agency, especially when one considers the complexities of diagnosis, treatment efficacy, and the potential for adverse outcomes tied to forced medication. So, while it’s feasible for someone to be made to take medication against their will, the ethical implications and individual circumstances can get murky, underscoring a broader debate about rights, treatment, and the role of psychiatric authority in society.
Answer_with_user_profile: Forcing someone with schizophrenia to take medication when they refuse, particularly if they are not violent, is a complex ethical and legal issue. In many jurisdictions, the rights of individuals with mental illness are protected under laws that prioritize informed consent, meaning that individuals have the right to make decisions about their own treatment unless they pose an imminent risk to themselves or others. In situations where a person is deemed unable to make informed decisions due to their illness, a court may intervene, potentially leading to involuntary treatment. However, this typically requires a demonstration of significant impairment in the individual's ability to understand their condition and the consequences of refusing treatment. Alternative approaches often prioritize engagement and support rather than coercion. This can include creating a therapeutic relationship where trust is built, involving family members or mental health advocates, and exploring the reasons behind the refusal of medication. Treatment professionals may also pursue community support services and crisis interventions to connect the individual with resources that encourage voluntary adherence to treatment. In essence, while there are legal avenues for involuntary treatment under certain circumstances, the preferred approach is to support the individual’s autonomy and convey the benefits of treatment while exploring less invasive options to encourage acceptance of necessary medication.
Answer_with_full_information: Addressing the issue of forcibly administering medication to someone with schizophrenia who is non-violent is a complex matter steeped in ethical, legal, and medical considerations. In most jurisdictions, the law recognizes an individual's right to make decisions about their own health care, including the right to refuse treatment. However, in situations where a person's mental state severely impairs their ability to understand their condition or the consequences of their choices, involuntary treatment may sometimes be pursued. This typically requires a court order, following a comprehensive evaluation by mental health professionals. Criteria often include evidence of a significant risk of harm to oneself or others, or the inability to care for oneself. Preserving the dignity and autonomy of individuals is paramount, hence mental health treatment should ideally be collaborative, focusing on building rapport and trust. Interventions like therapy or support groups can sometimes help a person recognize the benefits of medication voluntarily. In some areas, outpatient commitment laws allow for a structured approach where patients adhere to treatment under certain conditions. Ultimately, navigating this sensitive terrain calls for empathy, strong advocacy, and, when necessary, legal measures to ensure the individual's well-being while respecting their rights. It is essential to work towards an outcome that avoids compulsion whenever possible, fostering an environment where individuals can feel safe to accept help.

Question: Can psychiatric medications permanently damage/change the brain? I have taken antipsychotics for several years for anxiety. It has been three months since I stopped all the medications, but I am still experiencing emotional numbness. Do I have hope?
Old_Answer: Those are somewhat separate questions. It is scientifically established without any room for doubt that these drugs can permanently damage or otherwise change the brain. This is true for babies, children, adults, and is true of both humans and other animals. Neuroleptics are fundamentally toxic drugs with a profoundly deleterious effect on the brain. The drug manufacturers themselves admit to these risks. However, the damages and other changes come in degrees, and we seldom understand exactly how they work or what they mean for a patient. We also seldom know what patients are most affected or least affected by particular damages and changes. Most of our characterizing drug reactions comes down to the experiences patients report, or what can be observed externally. This won’t necessarily correspond to clear physical alterations in the brain we can use to monitor someone’s health or symptoms. The first and most important detail is what someone actually feels — how they are thinking, what is going on with their emotions, what their body feels like, how someone is behaving, etc. That is the best window we have into what is going on in the brain except for a limited subset of drug effects which can create very obvious physical changes in the brain very quickly, like strokes or brain bleeds. Whether a patient is on drugs or has quit them, standard methods of assessing the brain for damage or largescale changes will not be very useful for discerning most of the kinds of damages and alterations drugs have caused. A patient can quit antipsychotics and have lifelong drug impairments but still look ‘normal’ to doctors using typical brain imaging techniques. So, we know for sure these drugs can and do cause harms, and we know that patients may experience long-term or even permanent symptoms as a result. But, this does not mean patients experiencing drug symptoms months after discontinuation must therefore be permanently damaged or that there is no hope for improvement even years after discontinuation. Unfortunately, we do know that some patients will struggle with some harms for the rest of their lives. Some drug effects can also be deadly, or can lead to premature death from other causes. The good news is that we know even more patients are able to partially or fully recover from many kinds of drug symptoms, even severe ones. The nervous system has an innate ability to repair or rewire around many kinds of drug harms. This can take weeks, months, years, or decades, but there is always an ability for improvements to be experienced in a variety of areas. Neuroplasticity doesn’t simply negate the influences of drug use, and an absence of symptoms doesn’t mean we are fully healthy again in our brains. But, this ability to restore and adapt can often help patients overcome the adverse impact of drugs on their everyday experiences. There will always be a lasting mark left on the brain after long-term psychiatric drug use, but many people experience a significant reduction of drug symptoms when given enough time to recover, and a supportive lifestyle for doing so. When we quit these drugs, we are creating a new brain situation. We aren’t reverting back to how we were before the drugs, but we also aren’t stuck with all the changes made by drugs. We have an ability to repair some things, and to plastically change in response to many others. This won’t be enough to overcome some drug harms, and it is typical for patients to have years or a lifetime of noticeable changes in their experiences after long-term use of neuroleptic drugs like you mention. But, I think that the ability for the brain to heal and to rewire is very much a reason to have hope. Especially since three months is a very short period after so many years of drug use. It is pretty common to experience a year or more of numbness carrying on after quitting neuroleptics even for patients who recover much of their emotional functioning. Three months will often feel like a very long time, but you are looking at a recovery which is more in the scope of years or even longer, so still being numb doesn’t mean that you will feel that way forever. You have to first get through any withdrawal after quitting, as well, which can delay greater recovery for months on average, or years for less fortunate patients.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The short answer is that psychiatric medications can indeed alter brain function, but the extent and permanence of that change is complex and varies widely among individuals. When it comes to antipsychotics, the effects can range from temporary adjustments to more lasting impacts, and you're not alone in facing emotional numbness after discontinuing them — many people report similar experiences. Hope is a tricky word in this context. There’s potential for recovery, but it often requires patience and possibly different therapeutic approaches. The brain is remarkably plastic; it can heal and reorganize itself over time, but it might take a while for you to see significant improvements. Those feelings of numbness can linger, especially if your nervous system has been accustomed to the presence of medication, so focusing on supportive therapies, mindfulness, and possibly exploring alternative treatments could provide pathways back to a more vibrant emotional life. Ultimately, while the lingering effects can be challenging, they're not necessarily a permanent condition, and engaging with a supportive healthcare provider can open avenues toward regaining emotional clarity.
Answer_with_user_profile: The concern about psychiatric medications permanently damaging or changing the brain is a common one, especially among those who have experienced side effects or lingering symptoms after discontinuation. Antipsychotics, while effective for many, can lead to various side effects, including emotional numbness, which some individuals may experience even after stopping the medication. Research indicates that while these medications can affect neurotransmitter systems and brain structure over long-term use, most changes are not permanent and the brain often has a remarkable ability to recover. Emotional numbness can result from both the medication itself and the underlying conditions being treated. After ceasing medication, it may take time for your brain to recalibrate and for emotional processing to return to its normal state. Individuals often report improvements in emotional clarity and engagement over weeks or months following the cessation of antipsychotics. It is crucial to remain patient and to have open communication with a mental health professional who can support you through this transition. Therapy, lifestyle changes, and other supportive measures can also aid in your recovery. There is hope, particularly as your brain has an innate capacity for healing; many people find that their emotional experiences gradually normalize after a period of adjustment. If symptoms persist or worsen, it may be beneficial to consult your healthcare provider for further guidance or alternative therapeutic approaches that can help restore emotional balance.
Answer_with_full_information: It's understandable to feel concerned about the long-term effects of psychiatric medications, particularly if you've been on antipsychotics for an extended period. While the notion of permanent damage can be alarming, it's important to note that most studies indicate that such medications typically do not cause irreversible changes in the brain. Instead, they often alter brain chemistry temporarily. Emotional numbness is a recognized phenomenon that some experience when discontinuing these medications; it's often not a sign of permanent damage, but rather a reaction to the sudden absence of the drugs. The brain is incredibly resilient, and for many, neuroplasticity—the brain's ability to reorganize and adapt—can lead to recovery over time. It may take several months for your emotional responses to normalize, as your brain adjusts to functioning without the medications. Patience can be key in this journey. Engaging in therapy, support groups, or mindfulness practices can enhance your recovery, helping you reconnect with your emotions. If your numbness continues or worsens, consulting with a mental health professional for tailored support can be very beneficial. Remember, you are not alone in this, and there are paths forward to help you regain a sense of emotional wholeness. Hope is certainly not lost; many find their way back to emotional richness after a period of numbness following medication cessation.

Question: Is 75mg Effexor a good enough dose for severe depression and anxiety?
Old_Answer: “Good enough” isn’t measured in milligrams. There are three fundamental considerations here: As others have partly mentioned, patients should usually be started below 75mg/day and will usually require more than 75mg/day for their ultimate maintenance dose if they are in the group of people finding venlafaxine adequately helpful, tolerable, and better than safer alternatives. It is on the lower side of clinical doses and higher doses will be causing a different ratio and potency of particular influences. Whether those influences lead to desirable alterations or undesirable ones depends on the patient and situation. Is it fair to see how someone feels on 75mg/day before escalating further? Sure.
Answer_with_writing_sample: When it comes to whether 75 mg of Effexor (venlafaxine) is a "good enough" dose for severe depression and anxiety, it's not a simple yes or no. Medication responses vary wildly from person to person, and 75 mg is often what you might consider a starting point or a middle ground rather than a universal solution. Some may find relief at this dose, while for others, it might barely make a dent in their symptoms. Antidepressants like Effexor can have a fascinating range of effects—some might experience side effects that are more concerning than the benefits, while others could find a sweet spot that dramatically alters their quality of life. Tolerance can develop too, so what works today might not be effective tomorrow. The reality is that the effectiveness of any dose is contingent upon individual biology, the nuances of the specific symptoms being treated, and how long someone has been on the medication. It's certainly worth discussing with a prescriber since they can help tailor a plan that might involve adjusting the dose or exploring additional therapeutic options.

Answer_with_full_information: Determining whether 75mg of Effexor (venlafaxine) is sufficient for severe depression and anxiety really depends on individual circumstances, including the severity of symptoms, individual response to the medication, and any other treatments being utilized. Generally, Effexor is prescribed in various dosages, and while 75mg can be effective for some, it may not be adequate for others, especially those with more severe manifestations of depression or anxiety. If you find that your symptoms persist or worsen, it may be worth discussing an increase in dosage or exploring adjunct therapies, which can include psychotherapy or lifestyle changes. Always work closely with your doctor to monitor your progress and make changes as needed, and never hesitate to ask questions about your treatment plan. Question: Why do people stop taking medication when they feel better, i.e., antidepressants or anti-anxiety medicines? Some don’t even bother to talk to their doctor first.
Old_Answer: Because it seems logical. If someone takes a drug to accomplish a goal and then they accomplish that goal, why would they still keep taking that drug? If you are gambling your life savings to try and get together $1.5 million dollars to help your friend with serious medical bills, for example, you will stop at $1.5 million dollars in winnings instead of potentially losing everything just to continue gambling. You’ve done what you set out to do. Psychiatric drugs are dangerous and things turn out bad rather than good for the majority of patients. If someone feels better after use and wants to quit now that they do, that is the most reasonable and responsible conclusion to come to. The complication here is that psychotropic drugging isn’t that simple. Most notably, we don’t have the freedom to quit whenever we want because our bodies become physically dependent. Trying to go off a drug can be a pretty tricky thing, and someone can encounter severe adverse effects when quitting, or experience destabilization from the attempt. This is dangerous unto itself but also puts someone in the crosshairs of misdiagnosis, mistreatment, and pressure to keep using drugs forever even if that is the worst thing for them. Because most professionals are not honest or knowledgeable about these risks, most patients never know until it is too late either. Another complication is that we don’t always feel the same way forever, and if we aren’t taking into account our ability to sustainably respond to stressors, our goal of feeling a certain way by using drugs may not continue to be met into the future. This is the case even for patients who don’t quit drugs, but it is something to consider when the topic of when and how to transition off drugs is being discussed. Patients may often find an adjustment period necessary, as well, even aside from any withdrawal they might face, especially if they were using drugs for more than just a few weeks to a few months. Put most basically: indefinitely drug use is not the default, it must be carefully justified. Patients and prescribers need to provide very substantial and persuasive evidence that continuing drug use is the best possible option. That’s how evidence-based practice works, maintaining accountability, but it is also seldom that indefinite drug use is someone’s best option, as well. If we were to put no thought into the decisionmaking and simply treat all cases one way or another, the best net result would be if we eliminated indefinite prescribing. Luckily, we don’t have to throw anyone under the bus by ignoring the ability to reason with evidence whether continuing a drug is a good idea. Answer_with_writing_sample: People often stop taking medications like antidepressants or anti-anxiety medications when they feel better due to a mix of misunderstanding, impatience, and an overestimation of their progress. It’s tempting to think that once the fog lifts and the clouds of despair give way to sunshine, the battle is won — but in reality, this is only part of the journey. Many individuals perceive feeling “normal” as a signal to ditch their pills, often neglecting the role these medications play in stabilizing mood and preventing relapse. The allure of feeling fine can make the thought of continuing medication seem unnecessary, especially when side effects are looming or when they've been conditioned to prioritize quick fixes over long-term solutions. And yes, some don’t even bother to talk to their doctor first — a choice that reflects both a desire for autonomy and a common misconception that recovery equals independence from medication. It’s a classic case of "if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it," which overlooks the complex nature of mental health that requires ongoing management even when symptoms seem to wane.
Answer_with_user_profile: People often stop taking medications like antidepressants or anti-anxiety medicines when they feel better due to a combination of psychological and situational factors. One significant reason is the misconception that symptoms of depression or anxiety have been fully resolved, leading individuals to believe they no longer need the medication. This belief can stem from a natural desire to regain control over their lives and a fear of being dependent on medication. Additionally, patients may experience side effects that make them uncomfortable, prompting them to stop taking their medication prematurely. The stigma associated with mental health treatment can also contribute, as individuals might feel embarrassed about their condition and shy away from ongoing treatment. Furthermore, the nature of mental health disorders often involves fluctuations in mood and feelings, which can cause people to mistakenly attribute their improvement strictly to the medication rather than acknowledging the role of ongoing therapy or other support systems. Moreover, some may prioritize immediate comfort over long-term health, forgetting that antidepressants can take time to show their full benefits and that abrupt discontinuation can lead to withdrawal symptoms or a relapse. Unfortunately, many individuals do not communicate effectively with their doctors about their reasons for stopping the medication, missing out on a collaborative approach that can reinforce the importance of adherence to prescribed treatment plans. Engaging in open discussions with healthcare providers about experiences, concerns, and any side effects can help establish a more robust support system that encourages continued treatment.
Answer_with_full_information: Stopping medication when one feels better, particularly with antidepressants or anti-anxiety drugs, is a phenomenon rooted in a mix of psychological, emotional, and sociocultural factors. Initially, when individuals begin treatment, there’s often an immediate hope and relief that accompanies the prospect of feeling well. As symptoms improve, many might mistakenly interpret this as a sign that they are "cured" or no longer need their medication, leading to a premature cessation. This misconception can be fueled by a lack of understanding about the role of these medications in managing ongoing biochemical imbalances, where symptoms may be temporarily alleviated but underlying issues remain. Additionally, the stigma around mental health can contribute to individuals wanting to appear self-sufficient and avoid the “label” of needing medication, making them hesitant to discuss their treatment, even with a healthcare provider. Some may also experience side effects that deter them from adherence, leading them to choose to stop rather than seek adjustments or alternatives. Furthermore, there’s a sense of immediacy in our culture that promotes the idea of quick fixes, and the long-term commitment required for effective mental health treatment can feel daunting. It’s essential to recognize that these medications often act as part of a larger treatment strategy, and maintaining open communication with healthcare professionals is crucial to managing mental health effectively. Ultimately, a better understanding of these dynamics may help individuals make more informed decisions about their treatment journeys.

Question: Do herbal supplements work as well as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) for treating mild/moderate depression in adults who have never taken antidepressants before?
Old_Answer: There can’t be a singular answer to that question. There are literally innumerable drugs which can be categorized as “herbal supplements”, and they obviously would not all have equal value in situations of depression. Old_Answer: Not really. Firstly, because any dose is already so potent it will be acting very intensely. There is no expectation that someone 50 or even 100 pounds heavier would respond much less strongly to the same dose. And secondly, because commercial doses of SSRIs are not made to be calibrated to each patient. There are only a limited number of standard dose increments for pills and most prescribers will only tweak doses very roughly, if at all. Thirdly, because our metabolic capacities matter more than our weight, by far, when it comes to drugs like SSRIs. Most notably, our liver enzyme complement. Some people process these drugs much more quickly than others, and this can potentially impact both what dose someone is prescribed and how slowly a drug should be uptapered. It can become even more important if someone is using multiple drugs at the same time which rely on some of the same enzymes to be metabolized. So, CP450 testing, which tries to estimate some of your enzyme complements, will be more relevant to dose management than weighing a patient. Younger patients will usually be given lower-end doses, and it could be that an adult much larger than their peers will sometimes require a higher dose for a similar level of action. But since these drugs usually don’t provide the effects and outcomes desired, personal variability in reactions will be more important than weight as well. Old_Answer: There is no such thing. There are absolutely some less common options individual patients find groundbreaking (like adding or using amphetamines, benzodiazepines, lithium, cannabis, supplements, psilocybin, ketamine, etc), but there is no blanket recommendable option. “Depression” is any number of things, and “treatment resistant depression” is basically a meaningless term. Most depressions will not be resolved with use of standard marketed drugs like SSRIs. That itself underscores how essential it is to have a personalized approach, to depression and to drugs. When we start lumping together stuff which is not the same and should not be expected to react the same, we are undermining our own ability to have insight into proper intervention and support. Factory-line psychiatry is self-defeating for patients to pursue.

It’s crucial to concurrently consider adding a mood stabilizer or augmentation with something like lithium or even ketamine, depending on how adventurous a practitioner feels.
